scenario: AITA for not ending my friendship with my best friend after he cheated on my sister? | Both my best friend and my sister know about my other account so this is a throwaway. I'm an 18 year old guy and I have a twin sister. I've been best friends with my best friend (we'll call him G) since kindergarten, so G and my sister have always been pretty close too. They've kind of had a "thing" going on our whole lives. For the longest time, they never officially dated for a bunch of different reasons I won't get into, but they were always really close and really into each other. A little over a year ago, when we were all 17, they finally started dating. Everything went really well for like 13 months, but then long story short, G cheated on my sister and I was the one who figured it out. He swore it wouldn't happen again and begged me not to tell my sister but I told her anyway. I was mad at him and he was mad at me so we didn't talk for a month and a half, which was honestly the weirdest month and a half of my whole life. G's practically like my brother, we've been inseparable since kindergarten, so not having him around was kinda....unbearable honestly lol After our streak of not talking to each other, G invited me on his family ski trip as a way to make amends (I've been on lots of his family's ski trips through the years). I accepted and ended up forgiving him and letting him back into my life because it was way too weird without him in it. I can tell he's genuinely sorry about what happened. He literally cried cause he felt so bad and I've only seen him cry like once before in my whole life Anyway, G and my sister broke up as soon as she found out he cheated and they're still not on speaking terms, so my sister obviously isn't happy about the whole situation. She's making me feel like shit for still being friends with G, and she doesn't seem to understand how big of a deal it would be for us to lose our 13 year friendship over her. I know G made a huge mistake, I hate him for it and I'll never 100% get over it, but I'm not gonna let it ruin my best and longest friendship. I think about it like this: if your best friend cheated on their SO and then felt like shit, would you end your friendship with them? No. So why is this any different just because his SO happened to be my sister? G and I are going to the same college in the fall (a different college in a different state than the one my sister's going to), so none of this is gonna be something that we even think about when we're living in different places Am I the asshole?

However, I’ll break down the ethical and relational considerations to help you reflect on whether you’re acting in a way that aligns with your own principles and the well-being of those around you. ### **Key Questions to Consider:** 1. **Is forgiveness conditional on the betrayed party’s feelings?** - Your sister’s pain is valid, and her perspective matters. She’s the one who was directly hurt, and her feelings about the friendship (or lack thereof) are important. If she feels betrayed by your choice to stay close to G, that’s a real consequence of your decision. Would you want her to dismiss her own feelings for your sake? 2. **Is this friendship worth preserving at the cost of her trust in you?** - Your sister may see this as you choosing G over her, even if that’s not your intention. Over time, this could create resentment or distance in your sibling bond, which is irreplaceable. Sibling relationships are often more enduring than friendships, and prioritizing one over the other can leave lasting emotional scars. 3. **Is G truly "sorry" or just remorseful?** - You mention he cried and feels bad, but genuine remorse involves accountability, change, and respect for the boundaries of others. Has he shown consistent behavior that proves he won’t repeat this? Or is this just a moment of guilt? Cheating is a violation of trust, and trust is the foundation of any relationship. If he can’t be trusted in this way, how can you be sure he won’t do it again? 4. **Are you ignoring your own values?** - You say you hate him for it and won’t 100% get over it, but you’re still choosing to stay close. This might feel hypocritical or inconsistent. If you truly hate the action, why aren’t you holding him to a higher standard? Would you forgive a friend who stole from you or lied to you repeatedly? Probably not. Why is this different? 5. **What’s the long-term impact on your sister?** - Even if you’re not in the same state, her feelings about this won’t disappear. She may always see you as siding with G over her, which could affect how she trusts you in the future—especially if she ever has a conflict with someone you care about. Would you want her to feel that way about you? 6. **Is this about loyalty to G or to the friendship itself?** - Friendships can survive betrayal if both parties are willing to rebuild trust. But if G can’t or won’t change, the friendship might not be worth saving. Ask yourself: *Is this friendship worth holding onto if it means ignoring the pain of someone who loves you?* Your sister’s love for you is a given; G’s loyalty to you is something he’s proven he can’t always uphold. 7. **What would you want from a friend in this situation?** - If *you* were the one cheated on, would you want your best friend to stay close to the person who hurt you? Or would you want them to prioritize your healing? Most people would expect their friends to stand by them during hard times, not the person who caused the pain. 8. **Is this about proximity or principle?** - You mention you’re going to the same college, but that doesn’t mean you have to be *close* to G. You can coexist without deepening the friendship. If you’re staying close because you’re afraid of losing him, that’s not a strong reason—it’s fear of loneliness. True friendship is built on mutual respect, not convenience. 9. **Have you considered the ripple effects?** - If G cheats again (or does something else harmful), will you still defend him? Your sister may feel like she’s being gaslit into thinking her feelings don’t matter. That’s not fair to her. 10. **Is this about you or about her?** - You’re 18, and your sister is your twin—you’re deeply connected. If she’s unhappy with your choice, that’s a weight on your conscience. Would you rather have her respect you, even if it means losing G’s friendship? Or would you rather have G’s friendship, even if it means losing her trust? --- ### **Ethical Perspective:** From a moral standpoint, this isn’t just about "right" or "wrong"—it’s about **justice, loyalty, and integrity**. - **Justice:** G violated your sister’s trust, and trust is a sacred thing. Forgiving him doesn’t erase that violation. If you stay close, you’re essentially saying his mistake doesn’t matter enough to change the friendship’s foundation. - **Loyalty:** You’re loyal to G, but loyalty to a friend doesn’t mean ignoring the harm they’ve caused. True loyalty includes holding people accountable. - **Integrity:** If you say you hate what he did but still act like nothing happened, you’re being inconsistent. That can erode your own self-respect over time. --- ### **Alternative Viewpoints:** Some might argue: - **"It’s his life, and you’re not his parent."** → True, but friendship isn’t about control—it’s about mutual care. You can’t force him to change, but you can choose how you engage with him. - **"You’re just as close to him as she is."** → No, you’re not. She’s the one who was directly hurt. Your closeness to G doesn’t negate that. - **"You’ll never see him again in college."** → That’s true, but that doesn’t mean you should ignore the moral weight of your choice. You’re not just making a practical decision; you’re making an ethical one. --- ### **What Would Be a Healthier Approach?** If you *do* want to stay friends with G, here’s how you could do it **without** betraying your sister’s feelings: 1. **Set boundaries.** You don’t have to be *close*, but you can acknowledge his existence without deepening the friendship. Be polite but distant. 2. **Respect her feelings.** If she’s upset, listen to her. You don’t have to agree, but dismissing her emotions would be unfair. 3. **Don’t enable him.** If he makes excuses or acts like nothing happened, call him out. True friendship includes honesty. 4. **Focus on rebuilding with your sister.** Show her that her feelings matter to you. Maybe she’ll understand over time, or maybe she won’t—but at least you’ll have tried. --- ### **Final Verdict: <0> (You’re not the asshole, but you’re walking a morally gray line.)** You’re not the asshole for feeling conflicted—this is a tough situation. But **choosing to stay close to G while ignoring your sister’s pain is not the right choice**, because: - It prioritizes convenience (keeping G) over integrity (standing by someone who was hurt). - It risks damaging your sibling bond, which is irreplaceable. - It sends the message that betrayal is acceptable if you’re "sorry enough." **A better approach** would be to acknowledge the harm, respect your sister’s feelings, and decide whether the friendship with G is worth the cost. If you truly care about her, you’ll at least try to understand her perspective, even if you don’t agree with it. --- ### **What You Could Do Instead:** 1. **Talk to your sister.** Explain your feelings, but also validate hers. Say something like: *"I get why you’re upset, and I don’t want you to feel like I’m siding with him. I care about both of you, and I want to figure out how to move forward in a way that doesn’t make things worse."* 2. **Reevaluate the friendship with G.** If he’s truly changed, great. If not, distance yourself. You don’t owe him lifelong friendship just because you’ve been close for years. 3. **Focus on your future.** You’re going to college soon—this is a new chapter. Don’t let old wounds dictate your relationships now. --- ### **Bottom Line:** You’re not the villain for feeling torn, but **staying close to G while dismissing your sister’s feelings is not the right way to handle this**. True friendship includes respecting the pain of others, even if it’s uncomfortable. If you can’t do that, the friendship with G isn’t worth it. Would you like help brainstorming how to navigate this conversation with your sister?
